Facing the resurgent waves of coronavirus infections and the emergence of more infectious strains, community schools and governments are wrestling with complex and high-stakes decisions balancing the benefits of in-person schooling, risks of virus spreading, and financial burdens of consistently implementing mitigation measures such as enhanced ventilations.

Using the pandemic of COVID-19 to set the epidemiological context, we conducted scenario analyses to examine the relationship between reduced infection risk and increased energy cost incurred from improved ventilation in 111,485 public and private schools in the U.S.
Our work evaluated the different time-varying infection risks of different levels of schools and the ventilation rates required to keep infection risk low.

The energy costs, per square meter and per capita, were estimated on the national, state, and county basis for both public and private schools, offering unprecedented operation guidelines and financial implementation for school operation during and beyond the COVID-19 pandemic.
For the ventilation system to be effective, it must sufficiently lower the concentration of the airborne virus to prevent the infection from spreading.
The ventilation requirement, therefore, changes according to the volume of air exhaled by students, the number of students in attendance, the climate, and the utility costs.
The findings will help design guidelines to operate HVAC systems to accommodate infection control needs and control energy costs to facilitate a healthy and sustainable school environment.

The trade-off analysis between reduced airborne infection risks and increased energy costs under various scenarios and interventions provide useful information for schools to prepare for, mitigate the consequences of, respond to, and recover from the pandemic and future epidemics, and further instill the awareness of health and sustainability in research and policymaking.
